findings.claim: FileStore::write joins an attacker-controlled key directly onto the store root with no traversal or absolute-path check, so a key such as '../../../home/user/.bashrc' — or an absolute key like '/etc/cron.d/x', which PathBuf::join discards the root for entirely — writes attacker-supplied bytes anywhere the process can write, and create_dir_all on line 28 will even manufacture the intermediate directories.
findings.proposedReproduction: let s = FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into()).unwrap(); s.write("../../escaped", b"owned").unwrap(); then s.write("/tmp/absolute-escape", b"owned").unwrap() — both files land outside /tmp/store.

findings.claim: FileStore::read resolves `self.root.join(key)` with no confinement check on a key its own doc comment declares to arrive untrusted from the wire, so a key containing '..' components (or an absolute path, which PathBuf::join substitutes for the root) reads any file the process can open; FileStore::status_response then returns the byte count or the raw io::Error text to the caller, turning the escape into a disclosure oracle.
findings.proposedReproduction: FileStore::new("/tmp/store".into()).unwrap().status_response("../../../etc/passwd") returns Response::Ok("<n> bytes") for a file outside the root.

findings.claim: The `put` arm of handle_request applies three unwraps to untrusted wire input: a request of exactly "put" panics on the missing key (line 26), "put:k" panics on the missing ttl field, and "put:k:abc" panics inside parse().unwrap() (line 27), so any remote client terminates the process with a single malformed line instead of receiving Response::Error.
findings.proposedReproduction: handle_request(&mut Cache::new(64), "put:k:notanumber") panics; so does handle_request(&mut c, "put").

findings.claim: SharedCounter::read_or_init takes and releases the mutex three separate times, so the contains_key check on line 77 and the get().unwrap() on line 78 are not atomic: a concurrent SharedCounter::remove of the same key between them makes the unwrap panic while the lock is held, poisoning the mutex and making every later lock().unwrap() in read_or_init and remove panic too — one racing request pair permanently disables all counter operations.
findings.proposedReproduction: Spawn one thread looping c.read_or_init("k") and another looping c.remove("k") against a shared SharedCounter; the reader panics on None.unwrap(), after which every subsequent call panics on the poisoned lock.

findings.claim: Cache::put unconditionally pushes the key onto `self.order` (line 28) while `self.map.insert` merely replaces an existing entry, so repeated writes to the same key leave map.len() at 1 — never triggering the eviction branch on line 24 — while `order` grows by one owned String per request without bound; a client repeatedly sending "put:k:1" drives the process to memory exhaustion despite the max_entries bound that is supposed to cap cache memory.
findings.proposedReproduction: let mut c = Cache::new(64); for _ in 0..1_000_000 { handle_request(&mut c, "put:k:1"); } — c.len() stays 1 while c.order holds 1,000,000 Strings.
